clinicalPearls: A common lower respiratory tract infection of infants, typically under 2 years and peaking around 2-6 months, most often caused by respiratory syncytial virus (RSV).
Begins with upper respiratory symptoms (coryza, cough, low-grade fever) that progress over a few days to tachypnoea, wheeze, crackles, and increased work of breathing.
Diagnosis is clinical; routine viral testing, chest radiographs, and blood tests are usually unnecessary and can be misleading.
Management is supportive: ensure adequate hydration and feeding, maintain oxygenation, and provide gentle nasal suction as needed.
Bronchodilators, corticosteroids, and antibiotics are generally not beneficial in typical bronchiolitis and are not routinely recommended.
Apnoea can be an early and sometimes presenting sign, particularly in young or premature infants.
Risk factors for severe disease include prematurity, age under 2-3 months, congenital heart disease, chronic lung disease, and immunodeficiency.
Most cases are self-limiting over 1-2 weeks, though cough can persist longer.
reference.pathophysiology: Viral infection of the small airway epithelium causes inflammation, oedema, and necrosis of epithelial cells with increased mucus production. Sloughed cellular debris and mucus, together with airway wall swelling, partially or completely obstruct the small bronchioles. Because infant airways are narrow, this obstruction produces air trapping, hyperinflation, atelectasis, and ventilation-perfusion mismatch, leading to wheeze, hypoxaemia, and increased work of breathing.
additionalDifferentials: Congenital heart disease with heart failure
additionalInvestigations: Nasopharyngeal viral testing (mainly for cohorting or in severe/atypical cases)
Chest radiograph only if diagnosis is unclear or deterioration is unexplained
Blood gas in severe respiratory distress or impending failure
Capillary or venous blood tests only when a bacterial complication is suspected
redFlags: Apnoea or episodes of colour change
Persistent hypoxaemia or rising oxygen requirement
Severe respiratory distress: marked recession, grunting, nasal flaring, head bobbing
Inability to feed or signs of dehydration
Exhaustion, lethargy, or signs of impending respiratory failure
reference.prognosis: Most previously healthy infants recover fully within one to two weeks; a minority, especially high-risk infants, require hospitalisation, and some children have recurrent wheeze afterwards.
pitfalls: Overusing bronchodilators, steroids, or antibiotics that provide no benefit in typical disease
Relying on transient oxygen desaturation readings and over-treating stable, feeding infants
Missing apnoea as a presenting feature in very young infants
Ordering routine chest radiographs, which may prompt unnecessary antibiotics for atelectasis mistaken for infiltrate
management: Provide supportive care with maintenance of hydration and feeding, using nasogastric or intravenous fluids if oral intake is inadequate
Give supplemental oxygen for hypoxaemia and perform gentle nasal suction to relieve obstruction
Avoid bronchodilators, corticosteroids, and antibiotics, which are not beneficial in typical bronchiolitis
Monitor closely for apnoea and worsening respiratory distress, escalating to high-flow oxygen, CPAP, or mechanical ventilation as needed
Apply infection-control measures with hand hygiene and cohorting of RSV-positive infants
Offer RSV prophylaxis with palivizumab to eligible high-risk infants and give parents safety-net advice on warning signs
Have a low threshold for hospital admission of young, premature, or comorbid infants
